strengths: Theoretical framework of a two-layer neural network for more realistic data assumption.
A finite-degree polynomial model serves as an equivalent performance model.

The framework provides a novel lens for understanding neural networks trained on Gaussian mixture data with structured covariances, marking a clear advancement over previous works that lacked these structural considerations.

The paper includes a compelling mix of theoretical insights and numerical experiments, with applications to Fashion-MNIST classification. These experiments effectively validate the theoretical claims and underscore the significant impact of data structure on neural network learning outcomes.
The work is situated within recent literature seeking to quantify feature after a single aggressive gradient step in two-layer neural networks.
The main difference with respect to these works is the data model, which includes a multi-modal model with structured covariance.
The paper is well written; results are sufficiently discussed and put in context.
Section 6 provides ample intuition and discussion on the effect of the different parameters of the problem, allowing to illustrate and support the experimental results.
Although I did not carefully check the proof, technical results seem sound.
Technically, the analysis of conditional Gaussian universality to structured covariances is interesting and relevant to extend the stream of recent related works to more realistic data distributions.
The analysis of the joint scaling of \(\eta, \lVert \Sigma\rVert\) is interesting, and provides an insightful picture of the tradeoff.
I appreciated section 6, and in particular the discussion of the effect of the alignment between different covariance spikes.
weaknesses: The primary weakness lies in Assumption (A.3), which requires all Gaussian components in the Gaussian mixture model to be zero-centered, limiting theoretical advancement as it may be reduced to the isometric case.

The theoretical insights intended to guide the practical training of neural networks are unclear; the connection between the proposed data model and real‑world applications needs clarification, and the motivation for extending beyond existing Gaussian distribution assumptions remains ambiguous.
The numerical experiments would be more compelling if implemented on larger‑scale datasets, e.g., ImageNet.
Lack of a close comparison with the related literature on the technical part of the work.
Technical results heavily build on previous work (e.g., Ba et al., 2022; Dandi et al., 2023a,b) but lack sufficient discussion of these connections.
The paper leaves open natural questions beyond its current scope, such as establishing Gaussian universality for the considered distribution.
The title may be overstating the contribution and could be toned down to better represent the scope.
The work does not provide a description of the feature spectrum for a single‑index target function, unlike prior work (e.g., Moniri et al., 2023).
It does not reach a tight asymptotic expression for test and train errors.
Unclear whether the equivalence between \(\sigma\) and \(\hat{\sigma}_l\) holds for the full training procedure, including gradient step on the first layer.
Unclear why the zero‑mean assumption (A.3) is necessary or if it can be relaxed to accommodate non‑zero means.
Lack of specific discussion of how the equivalence mentioned in line 410 aids the analysis.
